name: Sengoku-period daimyo armies (1467-1615)

weightNotes.aggression: A century of endemic war between daimyo; Nobunaga's attack on Imagawa's camp at Okehazama (1560) and Hideyoshi's invasion of Korea (1592, 158,800 prepared across nine divisions) show the offensive habit (Okehazama, Korea invasion pages). High.
weightNotes.maneuver: Surprise and speed won Okehazama, and in Korea Konishi reached Hanseong on 10 June 1592, 18 days after landing at Busan (Korea invasion page). But much campaigning was castle-to-castle. Middling.
weightNotes.flanking: Encirclement occurred (Mikatagahara 1573: the Tokugawa-Oda force 'almost totally annihilated... after being encircled'), but most set battles were frontal clashes of retainer bands. Middling.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Castle warfare dominated: Odawara (1590) was a starvation siege, Takamatsu (1582) was flooded by diverting a river with dikes, Nagashino (1575) began as a siege (Odawara, Takamatsu, Nagashino pages). High.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Daimyo kept their own bodyguard (hatamoto) in hand; little evidence of a doctrinal reserve. Educated guess, low-middling.
weightNotes.scouting: Nobunaga found and struck Yoshimoto's camp at Okehazama; Takeda's vassals warned Katsuyori of Oda's arrival before Nagashino (Okehazama, Nagashino pages). Middling.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Basis: share of starting strength lost (killed, wounded, captured, missing) at the moment of withdrawal or break, never the battle total with pursuit. derived:breakpoint-quartile: mean of modelRules.breakpoint.loserCasualtyShareAtBreak.medieval mid 0.20 and gunpowder mid 0.26, grade C. Previous 0.4 came from Nagashino 1575, 10,000 of 15,000, a chronicle total including the pursuit (Nagashino page). Mixed evidence: retainer bands held long (Shimazu at Sekigahara) while armies collapsed through defection or loss of the lord at low losses (Okehazama, Sekigahara). Era baseline.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Ashigaru with arquebus, spear and bow in specialised units around mounted and foot samurai; at Nagashino Oda guns fought behind horse fences (the classic '3,000 guns in three ranks' is disputed; Nagashino, Ashigaru pages). 0.7.
weightNotes.initiative: Daimyo and their senior vassals commanded semi-independent contingents; the Sengoku period saw 'many instances of vassals rebelling against their lords' (Sengoku period page). High latitude, but unreliable.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Domestic campaigns were short and local; Hideyoshi kept a huge army supplied for a months-long starvation siege at Odawara, but in Korea the Joseon navy's attacks on supply fleets 'forced the Japanese forces to withdraw from the northern provinces' (Korea invasion page). Middling.

summary: Armies of regional warlords built from samurai retainer bands and increasingly from drilled ashigaru foot soldiers organised by weapon: arquebus (from 1543), long spear and bow, with mounted samurai as shock troops. Campaigns turned on castles, taken by starvation, mining or flooding, and on set battles often decided by surprise, the death of a commander, or defection of allies. Unification under Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and Ieyasu brought very large, well-supplied armies, field fortifications and massed firearms.
whyItWorked: Rapid adoption of firearms and specialised infantry units, combined with field works, let disciplined armies defeat brave but unsupported charges (Nagashino 1575). Leaders who struck fast at the enemy commander won out of proportion to numbers (Okehazama 1560). By 1592 Japan could ship and supply an army of about 150,000 and take the Korean capital in under three weeks.
whereItFailed: Cohesion rested on personal loyalty, so armies broke when the lord died (Okehazama) or allies changed sides (Sekigahara 1600). Overseas the system lacked naval control and logistics: Yi Sun-sin's fleet cut the supply line and Ming armies retook Pyongyang; by 1593 the invasion force was down from about 150,000 to 53,000, and the war ended with withdrawal in 1598.

sources.title: Conlan, State of War: The Violent Order of Fourteenth-Century Japan (2003)
